items.title: A Mamian Skirt Is Heavy and Easy to Twist: Who Should Buy One
items.excerpt: Flat panels front and back, pleats at the sides. Buy it if you will practice walking and sitting at home. Skip it if you commute, cycle, or sit all day and still expect the pleats to survive.
items.content:
The unkind version first. A mamian skirt is a nuisance. It is heavy. The waistband is thick. After you sit, the flat panel shifts and the pleats crush. It is hot in summer. Before you get into a car you have to lift the back panel onto the seat. A toilet stop is awkward. That is the garment, not your hands. A lot of what comes back to the shop was ordered off one front-facing photo.

The part people like is also real: a fairly flat panel, the “door,” on the center front and again on the center back, with the pleats at the sides so they move when you walk. “Horse-face” names those two panels. It is not a riding skirt. On a bicycle or in a packed train it gets in the way.

Who can buy one, and who should not

Buy it if you want that door-and-pleat shape and you will put it on at home, walk, sit, and take it off before you wear it out. Photos, a festival, two or three hours outside: it can do that. You accept the weight, and you accept one extra move before you sit in a car.

We would rather you did not buy it if:

  • You commute every day and still want the pleats intact at night. A full day of sitting shifts the doors and flattens the pleats. It will not look like the skirt you left in.
  • You want to throw it on without checking whether this one is two panels or one piece. Skip that check and the doors often end up at your sides, with a wall of pleats in front.
  • You overheat and you need to walk in the sun all day. The layers and the waistband do not breathe. It is not a summer skirt.
  • You only want the waistband hauled up high so your legs look longer. The hem shortens, the side pleats drag forward, and the doors leave the center line.

The heavy embroidered ones are pickier. Full embroidery, metallic yarn, and stiff interfacing add weight, and the pleats remember the direction they were set in. If you put it on twisted, an iron will not save it. If you want a skirt you can machine-wash and stuff in a bag, do not buy this. Washing is another piece. The short version: the prettier heavy ones are the worse ones to wash.

Spread it out. Our skirts do not all close the same way

Some are two panels that overlap. Some are one piece with a side opening. Where the tie passes through a loop is not the same from maker to maker, and our own stock is not standardized into “wind it three times.” There is no three-turn rule. Tighter is not better. If the ties hurt, the hem length changes and the pleats crush when you sit.

On correctly, it looks like one thing. The doors sit on the center front and center back, the pleats hang at the sides, the waistband is level, and you can breathe. Compare it with the sew-in label or the maker diagram: the panel with the fuller embroidery, an inside/outside label, a hidden snap, a loop, a side opening, the end the tie comes from. On two panels, decide which one faces out. On one piece, see which way the opening faces and whether the tie is meant to pass through a loop. If you cannot tell inside from outside, stop.

Jacquard, embroidery, and metallic yarn make the pleats more stubborn and the skirt heavier. If the pleats are in the wrong place, fix the overlap and the waist height first. Do not use hard steam to invent the pleat you wanted. A lot of synthetic and blended pleats are set in finishing. Press them wrong and they collapse for good.

An order that works on most ready-to-wear

If the note in the parcel disagrees, follow the note.

  1. Find the panel that should face out, and the ties or fasteners. Do not leave the ties twisted.
  2. Set the front door on the center of your body. Natural waist, or the height the maker marked. Hauling the skirt up to lengthen the leg shortens the hem and drags the side pleats forward.
  3. If there is a slit or a loop, pass the tie through it. Do not tear a hole in the cloth. If there is no opening, overlap the two panels the way they were cut.
  4. Bring the back door onto the center back. The two doors should sit at about the same height. Keep the waistband level.
  5. Settle the side pleats with your hands, in the direction they were pressed. Do not drag them onto the front to fake a wider door.
  6. Walk, sit, and lift a knee as if you were taking a stair. See whether the overlap gapes and whether a door has rotated. Firm enough to stay up. Loose enough to breathe. In a car, put the back panel on the seat before you sit.

If it is twisted, put it on again. Do not iron it

A wall of pleats in front and empty sides usually means the whole skirt has rotated, or the panels were swapped. Untie it and center it. An iron does nothing for that.

If the waistband slides down, check the overlap, the waist height, and the size. Do not pull the ties into the skin. Leave the knot at the side or the front.

After you take it off, undo the ties and let it air before it goes into a cupboard. Wet pleats under weight set hard creases. Embroidery can transfer dye.

One museum piece is not the only way a mamian may be worn today. Historical lower garments changed with period and occasion, and commercial skirts do not all close the same way. What is above is ready-to-wear you can wear out of the house. It is not a reconstruction of one dynasty.

The first time, do the whole cycle at home: on, walk, sit, off. Have someone look from the side. Doors in front, pleats at the side. If it does not suit you, do not force it at the event. This skirt does not owe anyone a promise that it looks right on every body and every day.

References: HanfuAuras — How To Wear A Ma Mian Skirt; Eastern Story — Ma Mian Qun Guide; HanfuAuras — How To Wear Hanfu; The Garment Atlas — Hanfu Etiquette.

items.title: Left Panel Over Right: Enough to Wear Out, Not a History of Every Collar
items.excerpt: On a living person, the left panel of a cross collar covers the right. That is enough for a wedding, New Year calls, and an ancestral hall. It is not a history of dress, and it does not fit a round collar.
items.content:
In the shop we teach one line for ordinary days: on a living person, the left panel of a cross collar covers the right. A wedding, New Year calls, an ancestral hall, and any day you mean to wear the robe out as Hanfu — that line is enough. It is not enough to write a history of dress. We do not use it to cover every dynasty.

The limit of the line should be said first. Collapsing a lot of periods into one direction is so you do not dress the way the dead were dressed. It is a shortcut, not an appraisal. Classical books, archaeology reports, and online tutorials do not always mean the same thing by youren and zuoren, “right lapel” and “left lapel.” In some texts “left lapel” is also tangled up with descriptions of other peoples’ clothing, and a slogan will not sort that out. Scholars are still discussing how cross collars actually opened in different periods. If the question is whether there was only ever one way, the shop cannot prove it.

Who the line is for, and who it is not for

It is for you if you bought a cross collar, you are going to meet people, and you do not want the overlap used for dressing the dead. In the mirror, the right panel goes against the body first. The left panel comes over it. Skip the right panel and just throw the left one on, and the neckline stays empty. The ties have nothing to work against. Lay the right panel flat, then cover it. The neckline sits against the neck: not choking, and not open enough to show a wide band of the inner robe. About one or two centimeters of the inner collar showing makes the layers easier to read. That is optional. Follow the overlap down to the side of the waist: the panel on top is your left, the right panel is underneath, and the side is not twisted into a rope. Some robes tie at the side, some slightly to the right of center front. Use the loops on this robe. Do not wind the ties into a hard knot at the back just to make them look symmetrical.

It is not for a round collar, a center-front opening, or a stand collar. Those are not cross collars, and this overlap does not apply. If a stage costume or a studio portrait reverses the collar for the picture, the description should say it is costume or a modern design, separate from wearing the robe out. At a funeral, if the family has its own arrangement, watch the room. Do not direct people with the shop’s everyday line.

The cross collars we sell are clothes made now. The overlap follows the custom people use now. The cloth is not a surviving textile from one dynasty. Polyester still has to close the same way. Closed correctly, it is still a modern robe. The overlap does not turn it into an old object.

Why burial dress closes the other way

The “Sang daji” chapter of the Liji says that in the lesser and greater dressings, sacrificial garments are not inverted, all are left-lapel, and the bindings are tied without loops. The traditional commentaries take this to mean the dead are dressed opposite to the living, because the ties will not be undone again. Zheng Xuan glosses it as “contrary to life.” If a living person deliberately closes an everyday cross collar that way, the Hanfu community treats it as a taboo, and at a wedding, at New Year, or in an ancestral hall it reads as rude.

The passage is about funeral dressing. It does not say that every robe in every dynasty could open in only one direction.

The neckline is seen before the pattern

On a formal occasion, do not wear the outer robe against bare skin. In hot weather the inner robe can be thin, but do not skip it. Sweat goes straight into the embroidery thread, and the outer cloth against skin is unpleasant. Before you sit, smooth the back hem with your hand and keep the knees together or slightly angled, so the pleats are not sat into a hard crease. Which hand goes on top in a salute depends on the occasion. At a funeral or a rite, watch what others do.

If the robe is too big, do not cross the panels all the way around to the back to make it fit. That twists the whole garment and wears hotter. Change the size, or take it in at the side loops the maker left. If it is too small, do not force the top closure. Horizontal strain across the chest looks worse than a neckline that sits a little easy.

At the door, raise your arms once and bend once. If the left panel flips and shows the inside of the right panel, snug the ties, or let the inner robe cover that gap. When you bend, the neckline should not open into a hole. That is more useful than inventing a “more ancient” overlap on the spot.

The tie can fool the mirror. For the left panel to stay on top, the knot is usually a little to the right of center front, or on the side loop the maker left. Move the knot to the left side of the waist and the left panel lets go. It looks reversed. It is the knot that moved. Put the knot back on the loop this robe was given, then judge left and right.

At a casual gathering, with no ancestral hall and no wedding, people may not mention a reversed collar. If the description says “worn the traditional way,” do not reverse it. A gathering and a rite are not the same thing. We also do not say a party is permission to reverse the collar and still call it the custom. A stage photo that reverses it should say it is costume. Worn out as Hanfu, the left panel stays on top.

Knowing the word youren, and never checking which panel is on top, means the robe is still wrong. One old image with the collar reversed, or one photograph of ethnic dress, is not an order that every Hanfu must close that way. Ask when the image was made, and what garment it is. A collar closed the usual way still looks careless if the cloth is crumpled and the neck is gaping.

References: Wikisource — Liji, Sang daji; Shidian — commentary on the left-lapel line in Sang daji; HanfuAuras — Respectful Engagement; The Garment Atlas — Hanfu Etiquette.

items.title: Heavy Embroidery Is a Pain to Wash. Say So Before Anyone Buys It
items.excerpt: The fuller the embroidery and the more metallic thread, the less it belongs in a washing machine. Buy it if you will read the label and hand-wash or dry-clean. If you want a machine cycle, buy a plain cloth, not the heavy work.
items.content:
The fully embroidered, brocaded, metallic-thread pieces in the shop are a pain to wash. No care slogan fixes that. The fuller the embroidery, the less it belongs in a machine. If the pleats were set in finishing, high heat collapses them and they do not come back. On these clothes, looking good and washing easily run in opposite directions. If you plan to throw it in with the sheets, do not buy the heavy work. Buy a plain cloth with no metallic yarn, no raised embroidery, and a label that allows a machine wash. After washing it will not look like the heavy piece. What you bought is convenience, not the same garment.

Who the heavy work is for, and who it is not for

It is for someone who will read the sew-in label, who can hand-wash or will pay for dry-cleaning, who has somewhere to dry it in the shade, and who will undo the ties after wearing so the damp can leave. Occasional wear suits it better than a commuting coat. Sweat, lipstick, and foundation at the collar have to be pressed out the same day with a soft damp cloth. Do not scrub.

It is not for someone who will not deal with the collar and who also will not accept “this cannot go in the machine.” It is not for someone who wants to practice laundry on old silk of unclear date. If it is already brittle or powdering, do not use the everyday wash below. Cloth mixed with leather and metal needs a person who cleans textiles. Do not soak it at home.

Silk does not mean a hand-wash will be fine. Dye and embroidery thread can be more fragile than the fiber. We do not promise that cool water makes it safe. If the care label or the maker’s card says dry-clean only, or do not wash, a forum tip loses.

Dry-cleaning is not a safety net either. Some solvents bite sequins, metallic thread, and fusible interfacing. Photograph the label and show it to the cleaner before you hand the piece over. If the label says do not dry-clean, do not gamble. No place to dry in the shade means the heavy work is wrong for you as well: a dryer’s heat collapses set pleats, and direct sun makes embroidery thread brittle. Without that space, do not buy it.

If the label allows water, do it this way

  • Cool water, or the low temperature the label permits. If the label gives no temperature, use cool water. Do not guess from how warm it feels on your hand. A mild detergent. Inside out, or in a mesh bag. Press the water out. Do not wring.
  • Dry in the shade, flat, or on a wide hanger that can carry the waistband. No hard sun. No hot dryer.
  • If you iron, low heat, through a cloth. Do not press straight onto raised embroidery or metallic thread. Leave set pleats alone.

A pleated skirt such as a mamian: undo the ties after wear, let it dry, then put it away. Do not park the same fold under weight for months. Wet pleats under pressure are how hard creases and dye transfer start. If you can only hang it, use a wide hanger under the waistband, doors facing out, pleats not bunched into one rope. If you must fold, follow the existing pleat direction, lay a clean cotton cloth in the fold, and do not pile a winter coat on top.

Embroidery thread and the ground cloth do not always shrink the same amount, so water can pull stitches. Metallic thread hates a sharp fold and a hard brush. Floating yarns in jacquard and brocade snag in a machine drum. Test a stain where it will not show. If it will not move, take it to someone who cleans textiles. Do not use chlorine bleach to “brighten” silk or rayon.

A ring at the collar shows up faster than mud on the hem. The day you get home, press a soft damp cloth on the mark. Do not rub back and forth. Blot food oil first, then decide whether the whole garment needs water. If an embroidered skirt is only soiled at the back of the knee, treat that spot. Do not soak the metallic thread for one patch of mud. After a wash, lay it on a dry towel and press the water out before you hang it. Do not shake it by a wet waistband. The pleats tangle and the embroidery pulls. Do not clip a peg onto the embroidery.

Old clothes and collections do not get this hand-wash

The Canadian Conservation Institute is plain: cleaning cannot be undone. Silk, wool, early man-made fibers, pieces with sequins or feathers, and textiles that are already brittle or powdering are not for a home soak. For an old garment of unclear date, keep the dust off and handle it less. If you must remove dust, vacuum on low suction through a screen, then ask a textile conservator. Do not run it through the everyday wash above.

Museum storage uses few folds, pads the folds so they are rounded, and does not stack weight on top. Silk and wool need caution around alkaline materials. Large pieces can be rolled. Raised embroidery is rolled face out so the stitches are not crushed. A home cupboard will not do that. Dry, out of the sun, aired, and with the embroidery not at the bottom of the pile is the part you can actually do. Vacuuming through a screen is not a substitute for washing a polyester mamian. Those are different jobs. High steam will not save set pleats. It destroys the pleat the factory set.

Before you buy, three questions. Can you hand-wash, or will you pay for dry-cleaning? Is there somewhere to dry it in the shade? Can you accept that it does not go in a machine? If one answer is no, do not buy the heavy work. We are not going to call a difficult garment easy.

References: CCI Notes 13/7 — Washing Non-coloured Textiles; CCI Notes 13/2 — Flat Storage; CCI — Caring for textiles and costumes; Eastern Story — Mamian care notes; HanfuAuras — Hanfu care notes.
